title: A Fall Can Carry a Signal

scenes.tts: A rod cell in your retina can register a single photon. It reports that photon by switching a current off. In the dark, the rod runs a steady inward current and releases transmitter without pause. Light reduces both. How can a fall carry a signal?
scenes.visual: A tall rod cell with green current arrows going in and a photon above it. Two traces draw flat (inward current, transmitter), then the photon drops in and both traces dip. A red arrow marks the fall and a dashed box asks: signal?
scenes.narration: A rod cell in your retina can register a single photon. It reports that photon by switching a current off. In the dark, the rod runs a steady inward current and releases transmitter without pause. Light reduces both. How can a fall carry a signal?

scenes.tts: In the dark, the rod contains a messenger called c G M P. It binds directly to cation channels in the membrane, with no kinase in between, and holds some of them open. Sodium and calcium flow in through those channels, and that inflow is the dark current. Because of it, the rod sits partly depolarized and releases glutamate continuously. The rod must maintain this baseline all through the dark.
scenes.caption: In the dark, the rod contains a messenger called cGMP. It binds directly to cation channels in the membrane, with no kinase in between, and holds some of them open. Sodium and calcium flow in through those channels, and that inflow is the dark current. Because of it, the rod sits partly depolarized and releases glutamate continuously. The rod must maintain this baseline all through the dark.
scenes.visual: Many cGMP chips float in the cell. A membrane with four channel gates appears, all shut. Three cGMP chips fly up and bind, and those gates swing open; sodium and calcium pour through. The flat traces on the right get a dashed baseline.
scenes.narration: In the dark, the rod contains a messenger called cGMP. It binds directly to cation channels in the membrane, with no kinase in between, and holds some of them open. Sodium and calcium flow in through those channels, and that inflow is the dark current. Because of it, the rod sits partly depolarized and releases glutamate continuously. scenes.tts: Rhodopsin, the rod's receptor, holds a bent molecule called retin-al. While retin-al is bent, the receptor stays off. A photon straightens the retin-al, and rhodopsin becomes active. Active rhodopsin switches on transducin, the rod's G protein, and transducin switches on a phosphodiesterase, P D E six. This enzyme destroys c G M P, a messenger that was already there.
scenes.caption: Rhodopsin, the rod's receptor, holds a bent molecule called retinal. While retinal is bent, the receptor stays off. A photon straightens the retinal, and rhodopsin becomes active. Active rhodopsin switches on transducin, the rod's G protein, and transducin switches on a phosphodiesterase, PDE6. This enzyme destroys cGMP, a messenger that was already there.
scenes.visual: The channel row moves up. Along the bottom a rhodopsin blob holds a bent-retinal chip; a photon hits, the chip becomes straight retinal and the blob goes active. Arrows run to transducin and then PDE6, which rises into the cGMP chips and destroys them one by one, leaving dashed ghosts.
scenes.narration: Rhodopsin, the rod's receptor, holds a bent molecule called retinal. While retinal is bent, the receptor stays off. A photon straightens the retinal, and rhodopsin becomes active. scenes.tts: So c G M P falls, and the channels close. The inward current shrinks, and the membrane hyperpolarizes. Glutamate release drops, and the next cell reads that drop. In a toad rod, the dark current is roughly twenty picoamps. Each rhodopsin that a photon turns dips that current by about one picoamp.

scenes.visual: A cGMP level gauge drains while the three open gates swing shut and the ion flow stops. Two big traces below fall at once (inward current, glutamate). A next-cell chip reads the glutamate drop; labels give roughly 20 pA and a dip of about 1 pA.

scenes.tts: The nose works the other way round. Each sensory neuron in the nose has just one receptor, chosen from a very large family. An odorant binds its receptor, and a G protein then switches on an enzyme, adenylyl cyclase. The messenger c A M P rises, and it directly opens a cation channel related to the rod's. The neuron depolarizes and fires.
scenes.caption: The nose works the other way round. Each sensory neuron in the nose has just one receptor, chosen from a very large family. An odorant binds its receptor, and a G protein then switches on an enzyme, adenylyl cyclase. The messenger cAMP rises, and it directly opens a cation channel related to the rod's. The neuron depolarizes and fires.
scenes.visual: The same shut channel row, now empty of messenger. An odorant binds a receptor, then a G protein, then adenylyl cyclase; cAMP chips pour up from the cyclase, three bind the channels and the gates swing open. A voltage trace rises and spikes.
scenes.narration: The nose works the other way round. Each sensory neuron in the nose has just one receptor, chosen from a very large family. An odorant binds its receptor, and a G protein then switches on an enzyme, adenylyl cyclase. The messenger cAMP rises, and it directly opens a cation channel related to the rod's. The neuron depolarizes and fires.

scenes.tts: In the rod, light makes c G M P fall. In the nose, a smell makes c A M P rise. In an artery wall, nitric oxide makes that same c G M P rise, and the muscle relaxes. Keep this rule. A signal is a change from a baseline, and a cell can read a change in either direction.
scenes.caption: In the rod, light makes cGMP fall. In the nose, a smell makes cAMP rise. In an artery wall, nitric oxide makes that same cGMP rise, and the muscle relaxes. Keep this rule. A signal is a change from a baseline, and a cell can read a change in either direction.
scenes.visual: Three rows, each with a dashed baseline: rod (cGMP falls), nose (cAMP rises), artery wall (the same cGMP rises, muscle relaxes). The two cGMP rows are linked; then the baselines glow and a two-way arrow marks a change in either direction.
scenes.narration: In the rod, light makes cGMP fall. In the nose, a smell makes cAMP rise. In an artery wall, nitric oxide makes that same cGMP rise, and the muscle relaxes. Keep this rule. A signal is a change from a baseline, and a cell can read a change in either direction.
